extracted.intended_audience: ship designers, marine engineers, naval architects, and ship managers
extracted.subtask_description: A catalogue of required properties and design criteria for marine engines and ship arrangements (fuel economy, reversibility, seaworthiness, accessibility, vibration control, passenger comfort, measurement and operational requirements) as described in a 1907 Nature lecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engine must be reversible
rubrics_metrics.description: The engine must be reversible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the first essential condition for any successful marine engine of any type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid stop and quick ahead/astern starting
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be capable of being stopped quickly, and of being started quickly either ahead or astern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises operational responsiveness required for manoeuvring and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth, prompt, and steady speed control across full range
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be capable of being promptly speeded to any desired number of revolutions between dead slow and full speed, and of being kept steadily at the required speed for any length of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'dead slow' as not faster than one-quarter of full speed (and should be less in very fast vessels), stressing fine control from very low to full speed and sustained steadiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous reliability over long runs
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be capable of running continuously for long distances, with but short intervals between the runs, without risk of stoppage or breakdown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational reliability and durability for long voyages with minimal downtime is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective operation in both smooth and heavy weather
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be capable of working well, not only in smooth water, but also in heavy weather in a seaway, where the varying immersion of the propeller causes rapidly changing conditions of resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engine and propulsion must tolerate rapidly changing loads due to seaway conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and maintainability of working parts
rubrics_metrics.description: All working parts must be readily accessible for overhauling, and all wearing surfaces must be capable of being promptly and easily adjusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must permit quick maintenance and adjustment of wearing components to minimize downtime and maintenance effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel economy at ordinary working speed
rubrics_metrics.description: The engine must be economical in fuel, especially at its ordinary working speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fuel consumption is a chief point for ocean liners; later text gives benchmarks (e.g., quadruple-expansion engines with 210–220 lb boiler pressure achieving ~13 lb coal per I.H.P. per hour) and stresses that substitution of turbines depends chiefly on matching such low consumption figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness, low weight, and balance to avoid vibration
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be compact, light in weight, and well balanced so as not to cause vibration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight and balance trade-offs affect efficiency and vibration; designers often sacrifice some maximum efficiency to reduce weight in classes where weight is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: No risk of hazardous gas accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: It must not involve any risk of accumulation of gas in the ship such as could form an explosive mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety requirement for any fuel/engine system to avoid explosion hazards aboard ship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fuel with practically unlimited, affordable, and globally available supply
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a sine qua non that it must be capable of using a fuel the supply of which at moderate price is practically unlimited, and that could be obtained readily in whatever part of the world a ship might happen to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistical/fuel-supply requirement: fuel must be widely obtainable at reasonable cost to support worldwide operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate measurement of turbine power/torque
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct measurement of the power given out by turbine machinery is a practical problem of great importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telephonic recording apparatus indicating shaft twist over a length has had some success in measuring torque, but records are not always as definite and accurate as desired; a satisfactory solution to torque/power measurement is much required by ship designers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metallurgical and mechanical resistance for large internal-combustion cylinders
rubrics_metrics.description: Large cylinders must be produced which will stand the high impulses and great and rapid variations of temperature that occur with internal combustion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until engineers and metallurgists overcome these difficulties, major steps toward large-size internal-combustion marine engines cannot be taken; emphasises materials and durability constraints for IC marine propulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oil-fuel systems must be efficient and economical
rubrics_metrics.description: Oil fuel systems (spraying liquid for combustion by hot air) have achieved great practical advance; consumption as low as 0.9 lb per I.H.P. per hour has been regularly realised in mercantile vessels employing spray systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combined systems (high and low pressure air for desiccating/pulverising and assisting combustion) have proved highly successful and economical; operational evidence from long voyages supports viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for passenger comfort: steadiness and minimal rolling/pitching
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide steadiness at sea, and freedom from heavy rolling and pitching; metacentric height regulation and suitable stowage/ballast are important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designer can help by suitable metacentric height (about 18 inches appears to give a satisfactory combination in large ships); final regulation at sea by stowage and water ballast requires careful attention by ship's officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bilge keels to increase rolling resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Bilge keels, opposing their surface to rolling motion, are very effective in reducing rolling extent when of sufficient depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ships fitted after building with suitably formed and placed bilge keels, extreme angles of rolling have been reduced to one-half; bilge keels are well known and admitted in the mercantile marine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of free-water chambers and pendulum/viscous-damper devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices using free water chambers or heavy pendulums in viscous fluid have been tried to check rolling, with mixed results dependent on timing/regulation and space/other objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free-water chambers gave good results within limits when water motion was well timed but were dropped (possibly for space/regulation objections). M. Victor Cremleu's pendulum-in-viscous-fluid and simplified transverse weight ideas propose opposing rolling by statical moment and dissipating energy as heat; such devices require careful design of clearances and fluid viscosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gyroscopic stabilisers as promising steadying apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Gyroscopic action devices (Dr. Otto Schlick's apparatus) appear promising for increasing resistance to rolling and are ripe for application to smaller classes of steamers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard electrically driven gyroscope (or steam-turbine driven where electric power margin is insufficient) is being designed for vessels ~1200–3000 tons; may be applicable to Channel steamers and similar classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation of pitching through hull form and accommodation placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Design forward transverse sections to best resist plunging into the sea; place passenger accommodation near the middle third of the ship to minimise pitching effects on passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitching period and axis vary with sea conditions; concentrating first-class accommodation mid-length reduces vertical motion experienced by passengers (about one-third of motion at ends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vibration control by balancing and structural reinforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent vibration by balancing principal working parts of reciprocating engines, ensuring true and balanced propeller blades, and stiffening/supporting vibrating plating areas with brackets or struts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations show how reciprocating engines cause vibration and how to reduce it; propeller-induced hammering on stern-plating can be checked by strong bracket frames, and sympathetic vibration in flat plating (decks, side-plating, bridges) can be overcome by careful attention to vibrating surfaces and local stiffening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose ship size and speed suited to trade economics
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a size and speed most appropriate and profitable for each line of steamers or trade; these are determined by managers who know passenger/cargo demand and profitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power required per ton diminishes with increasing size and working expenses per ton fall; designers should produce designs fulfilling size, draught, speed, capacity, and accommodation at minimum cost. Speed is limited by economic considerations: for many trades speeds above ~12–13 knots require extra expenditure to be paid from passengers or mail subsidy, not cargo freight.
